scenes.title: EXCEPT
scenes.narration: The EXCEPT operator returns the rows from the first query that do not appear in the second, giving you the set difference.

scenes.title: How EXCEPT works
bullets: It keeps rows in the first set that are absent from the second.
The result contains distinct rows only.
The order of the two queries matters.
scenes.narration: EXCEPT takes the rows produced by the first query and removes any that also appear in the second query. The result is a set of distinct rows, so duplicates are collapsed. Crucially the order matters, because subtracting set B from set A is not the same as subtracting A from B.

scenes.title: INTERSECT versus EXCEPT

right.title: EXCEPT
points: Rows in the first but not the second

scenes.narration: INTERSECT gives you the overlap, the rows shared by both sides, and it does not care which query comes first. EXCEPT gives you the difference, the rows in the first set that are missing from the second, so swapping the queries changes the answer. Together they cover the common cases of comparing two result sets.

scenes.title: Customers who left this year
scenes.code:
SELECT customer_id
FROM orders_2024

EXCEPT

SELECT customer_id
FROM orders_2025;
scenes.narration: The first query lists customers who ordered in twenty twenty four, and the second lists those who ordered in twenty twenty five. EXCEPT keeps only the customers from twenty twenty four who did not return in twenty twenty five. This neatly identifies churned customers who stopped buying.

scenes.text: PostgreSQL, SQL Server, and SQLite spell this operator EXCEPT, while Oracle calls it MINUS. Both mean the same set difference between two result sets.
scenes.narration: Be aware that PostgreSQL, SQL Server, and SQLite use the keyword EXCEPT, whereas Oracle spells the identical operation MINUS. Both compute the same set difference between two queries.
